claim: Phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI(3)P) levels in Plasmodium falciparum correlate with tolerance to cellular stresses caused by artemisinin and environmental factors.
source: Phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI(3)P) levels in Plasmodium falciparum correlate with tolerance to cellular stresses caused by artemisinin and environmental factors.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous work (Mbengue et al., 2015) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: PI(3)P stabilizes the digestive vacuole (DV) under heat stress in P. falciparum.
source: Live cell microscopy using chemical and genetic reporters revealed that PI(3)P stabilizes the digestive vacuole (DV) under heat stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live cell microscopy experiments shown in Figures 2, 3, and 5.

claim: Heat-induced DV destabilization in PI(3)P-deficient P. falciparum precedes cell death.
source: We demonstrate that heat-induced DV destabilization in PI(3)P-deficient P. falciparum precedes cell death and is reversible after withdrawal of the stress condition and the PI3K inhibitor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from JC-1 mitochondrial membrane potential assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: Heat-induced DV destabilization in PI(3)P-deficient P. falciparum is reversible after withdrawal of the stress condition and the PI3K inhibitor.
source: We demonstrate that heat-induced DV destabilization in PI(3)P-deficient P. falciparum precedes cell death and is reversible after withdrawal of the stress condition and the PI3K inhibitor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 demonstrating recovery of DV membrane integrity.

claim: PfHsp70-1 is a PI(3)P-binding protein.
source: A chemoproteomic approach identified PfHsp70-1 as a PI(3)P-binding protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data (Table 1) and protein-lipid overlay assays (Figure 6).

claim: An Hsp70 inhibitor phenocopies PI(3)P-deficient parasites under heat shock.
source: An Hsp70 inhibitor and knockdown of PfHsp70-1 phenocopy PI(3)P-deficient parasites under heat shock.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using 15-DSG shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Knockdown of PfHsp70-1 phenocopies PI(3)P-deficient parasites under heat shock.
source: An Hsp70 inhibitor and knockdown of PfHsp70-1 phenocopy PI(3)P-deficient parasites under heat shock.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using the conditional PfHsp70-1 knockdown strain shown in Figure 7B.

claim: PfHsp70-1 downregulation hypersensitizes parasites to heat shock.
source: Furthermore, PfHsp70-1 downregulation hypersensitizes parasites to heat shock and PI3K inhibitors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 4B.

claim: PfHsp70-1 downregulation hypersensitizes parasites to PI3K inhibitors.
source: Furthermore, PfHsp70-1 downregulation hypersensitizes parasites to heat shock and PI3K inhibitors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: P. falciparum at the ring stage is more refractory to heat stress when compared to trophozoite and schizont stages.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that P. falciparum at the ring stage is more refractory to heat stress when compared to trophozoite and schizont stages (Kwiatkowski, 1989; Porter et al., 2008; Engelbrecht and Coetzer, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cyclical fever in patients with P. falciparum malaria often reaches 39–41°C and persists until the early schizont stage.
source: However, cyclical fever in patients with P. falciparum malaria often reaches 39–41°C and persists until the early schizont stage (Crutcher and Hoffman, 1996; Neva and Brown, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Artemisinin and its derivatives exert their antimalarial activity by generating carbon-centered radicals that cause oxidative stress and subsequent protein alkylation.
source: Artemisinin and its derivatives exert their antimalarial activity by generating carbon-centered radicals that cause oxidative stress and subsequent protein alkylation (Tilley et al., 2016; Paloque et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on artemisinin mechanism of action.

claim: Increased artemisinin resistance has been found in P. falciparum parasites with Pfkelch13 mutations.
source: Increased artemisinin resistance has been found in P. falciparum parasites with Pfkelch13 mutations (Miotto et al., 2015; Ariey et al., 2014; Ghorbal et al., 2014; Straimer et al., 2015; Mbengue et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on artemisinin resistance.

claim: PfKelch13 could modulate the level of PI(3)P through interaction with PfPI3K.
source: A previous study found that PfKelch13 could modulate the level of a signaling molecule phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI(3)P) through interaction with PfPI3K (Mbengue et al., 2015), while other studies did not detect the interaction between PfKelch13 and PfPI3K (Siddiqui et al., 2020; Gnädig et al., 2020; Birnbaum et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mbengue et al., 2015, but is also noted to be contradicted by other studies.

claim: PfKelch13 mutations have been linked to the accumulation of PI(3)P in P. falciparum-infected RBCs.
source: PfKelch13 mutations have been linked to the accumulation of PI(3)P in P. falciparum-infected RBCs and this increased PI(3)P level is highly correlated with parasite resistance to artemisinin (Mbengue et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mbengue et al., 2015.

claim: Increased PI(3)P level is highly correlated with parasite resistance to artemisinin.
source: PfKelch13 mutations have been linked to the accumulation of PI(3)P in P. falciparum-infected RBCs and this increased PI(3)P level is highly correlated with parasite resistance to artemisinin (Mbengue et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mbengue et al., 2015.

claim: Increasing PI(3)P levels by ectopically expressing a human PI3K, Vps34, in P. falciparum confers artemisinin resistance.
source: Increasing PI(3)P levels by ectopically expressing a human PI3K, Vps34, in P. falciparum confers similar resistance (Mbengue et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mbengue et al., 2015.

claim: A phenotypic screen using piggyBac mutagenesis showed a reduced heat tolerance in a pfkelch13-upregulated P. falciparum mutant.
source: Intriguingly, a phenotypic screen using piggyBac mutagenesis showed a reduced heat tolerance in a pfkelch13-upregulated P. falciparum mutant (Thomas et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2016.

claim: PI(3)P is a multifunctional lipid regulator that controls vesicular trafficking, protein sorting and autophagy in many model organisms.
source: PI(3)P is a multifunctional lipid regulator that controls vesicular trafficking, protein sorting and autophagy in many model organisms (Mayinger, 2012; Balla, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to reviews on PI(3)P function.

claim: The Plasmodium genome encodes a single PI3K that primarily synthesizes PI(3)P and is essential for intraerythrocytic parasite growth.
source: The Plasmodium genome encodes a single PI3K that primarily synthesizes PI(3)P and is essential for intraerythrocytic parasite growth (Tawk et al., 2010; Vaid et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Plasmodium PI3K.

claim: During the intraerythrocytic cycle, P. falciparum generates more PI(3)P at the trophozoite and schizont stages.
source: During the intraerythrocytic cycle, P. falciparum generates more PI(3)P at the trophozoite and schizont stages where this lipid localizes to the apicoplast and the digestive vacuole (DV) (Tawk et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tawk et al., 2010.

claim: PI(3)P localizes to the apicoplast and the digestive vacuole (DV) in P. falciparum.
source: During the intraerythrocytic cycle, P. falciparum generates more PI(3)P at the trophozoite and schizont stages where this lipid localizes to the apicoplast and the digestive vacuole (DV) (Tawk et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tawk et al., 2010.

claim: Lysosomes may undergo membrane destabilization in response to different stresses, which can lead to programmed cell death or necrosis.
source: In mammalian cells, lysosomes may undergo membrane destabilization in response to different stresses, which can lead to programmed cell death or necrosis (Olson and Joyce, 2015; Kirkegaard and Jäättelä, 2009; Li and Kane, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on lysosomal membrane permeabilization.

claim: The molecular function of PI(3)P in hemoglobin trafficking to the DV has been reported.
source: Although the molecular function of PI(3)P in hemoglobin trafficking to the DV has been reported (Vaid et al., 2010), its potential role in modulating Plasmodium stress responses has not yet been investigated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vaid et al., 2010.

claim: Heat shock for up to 6 hr resulted in no significant reduction in parasite growth/survival.
source: However, heat shock for up to 6 hr resulted in no significant reduction in parasite growth/survival (3 hr HS: p=0.27, 6 hr HS: p=0.12), indicating an intrinsic capacity of mature stage parasites to tolerate heat stress (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Prolonged heat shock (≥9 hr) led to a 32–41% reduction in parasite loads compared to the non-heat-shocked control.
source: Prolonged heat shock (≥9 hr) led to a 32–41% reduction in parasite loads (p<0.05, unpaired t-test) compared to the non-heat-shocked control (0 hr HS).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Wortmannin and LY294002 have been shown to reduce PI(3)P levels in P. falciparum and Toxoplasma gondii.
source: Two compounds with different chemical scaffolds, Wortmannin and LY294002, have been shown to reduce PI(3)P levels in P. falciparum and Toxoplasma gondii (a closely related parasite) (Mbengue et al., 2015; Tawk et al., 2010; Bansal et al., 2017; Dalal and Klemba, 2015; Tawk et al., 2011; Kitamura et al., 2012; Besteiro et al., 2011; Stutz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Upon heat shock, Wortmannin decreased parasite loads by 48 ± 32% compared to non-heat shock treatment.
source: Upon heat shock, Wortmannin and LY294002 decreased parasite loads by 48 ± 32% and 18 ± 10%, respectively, compared to non-heat shock treatment (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Upon heat shock, LY294002 decreased parasite loads by 18 ± 10% compared to non-heat shock treatment.
source: Upon heat shock, Wortmannin and LY294002 decreased parasite loads by 48 ± 32% and 18 ± 10%, respectively, compared to non-heat shock treatment (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A two-fold decrease in the LY294002 EC50 value was detected after heat shock.
source: To further demonstrate that PI(3)P deficiency renders parasites heat intolerant, we performed a standard dose response study with 6 hr heat exposure at the trophozoite stage. We detected a two-fold decrease in the LY294002 EC50 value after heat shock (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: LY303511 inhibited P. falciparum, but this inhibition was not heat-dependent.
source: To control for possible off-target effects of the compound, we also tested an inactive LY294002 analog, LY303511, which does not disrupt P. falciparum PI(3)P levels (Mbengue et al., 2015). LY303511 inhibited P. falciparum, but this inhibition was not heat-dependent (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and citation to Mbengue et al., 2015.

claim: Wortmannin showed a ~ 1.3 fold decrease in the EC50 value with heat exposure immediately after Wortmannin addition.
source: Wortmannin was similarly tested in our assay, but an EC50 shift was not observed using our standard assay format (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), possibly due to compound instability in complete medium (Tawk et al., 2010). Indeed, using another format with heat exposure immediately after Wortmannin addition resulted in a ~ 1.3 fold decrease in the EC50 value (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Atovaquone, pyrimethamine, quinacrine and lapachol did not exhibit a drug sensitivity change with heat exposure.
source: In contrast, a range of antimalarial drugs including atovaquone (electron transport inhibitor), pyrimethamine (folate synthesis inhibitor), quinacrine (unresolved mechanism) and lapachol (unresolved mechanism) did not exhibit a drug sensitivity change with heat exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: PI(3)P levels in P. falciparum parasites increased by 1.3–2.3 fold with heat shock.
source: Intriguingly, PI(3)P levels in P. falciparum parasites increased by 1.3–2.3 fold with heat shock, while uninfected RBCs exhibited no change after heat shock (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Uninfected RBCs exhibited no change in PI(3)P levels after heat shock.
source: Intriguingly, PI(3)P levels in P. falciparum parasites increased by 1.3–2.3 fold with heat shock, while uninfected RBCs exhibited no change after heat shock (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: No aberrant DV morphology or PM2GT mislocalization was found after a 6 hr heat shock in DMSO control.
source: No aberrant DV morphology or PM2GT mislocalization was found after a 6 hr heat shock, demonstrating the intrinsic stability of the DV during heat shock (p=0.64; Figure 2, DMSO control).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Wortmannin treatment resulted in a high background signal and PM2GT mislocalization even at 37°C.
source: Next, we examined if chemically inhibiting PI(3)P production affects DV membrane stability and morphology. However, Wortmannin treatment resulted in a high background signal and PM2GT mislocalization even at 37°C (no heat shock), making it difficult to identify heat-dependent changes (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: LY294002-treated parasites showed normal DV morphology and PM2GT localization at 37°C.
source: In contrast, LY294002-treated parasites showed normal DV morphology and PM2GT localization at 37°C, with DV MFIs comparable to the DMSO control (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: PM2GT redistributed out of the DV after heat shock in LY294002-treated parasites.
source: Interestingly, PM2GT redistributed out of the DV after heat shock, concomitant with a reduction in DV-localized GFP signal (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: LY303511-treated parasites did not show PM2GT redistribution or reduced DV signal after heat shock.
source: These changes were not observed with the inactive LY294002 analog (LY303511).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: 6 hr heat shock did not affect DV integrity in DMSO control parasites as measured by LysoTracker Red accumulation.
source: In agreement with our PM2GT experiment, 6 hr heat shock did not affect DV integrity (p=0.12; Figure 3A–C, DMSO control).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Both Wortmannin and LY294002 destabilized the DV after heat shock as measured by LysoTracker Red accumulation.
source: However, both Wortmannin and LY294002 destabilized the DV after heat shock (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: LY303511-treated parasites showed DV signals comparable to the DMSO control with or without heat shock.
source: In contrast, LY303511-treated parasites showed DV signals comparable to the DMSO control with or without heat shock.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Lapachol, atovaquone and pyrimethamine had no effect on DV stability at 37°C and 40°C.
source: Three representative compounds (lapachol, atovaquone and pyrimethamine) with different modes of action and potencies ranging from 1 nM to 46 μM had no effect on DV stability at 37°C and 40°C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: Artesunate induced heat shock-dependent DV destabilization.
source: We also tested an artemisinin-related compound, artesunate, and found that it induced heat shock-dependent DV destabilization (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Artemisinin and its analogs have been reported to disrupt PI(3)P levels in P. falciparum parasites.
source: Intriguingly, like Wortmannin and LY294002, artemisinin and its analogs have been reported to disrupt PI(3)P levels in P. falciparum parasites (Tilley et al., 2016; Mbengue et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is no correlation between DV MFI reduction and the fold EC50 concentrations (antimalarial potency) applied in this study.
source: Based on our microscopy data, there is no correlation between DV MFI reduction and the fold EC50 concentrations (antimalarial potency) applied in this study (p=0.34, Pearson's correlation coefficient r = −0.47; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with the proposal that DV permeabilization is triggered by reduced PI(3)P levels and not a general stress response.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Mitochondria remained polarized after LY294002 and heat treatments.
source: Our data show that mitochondria remained polarized after LY294002 and heat treatments, as revealed by their JC-1 red/green ratios compared to the DMSO controls (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mitochondrial membrane depolarization was observed in ~55% of the Wortmannin-treated parasites after heat shock.
source: In contrast, mitochondrial membrane depolarization was observed in ~55% of the Wortmannin-treated parasites after heat shock (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: >70% of the parasites showed DV membrane destabilization following Wortmannin treatment and heat shock.
source: From LysoTracker loading experiments, >70% of the parasites showed DV membrane destabilization following the same treatment, which suggests that a sub-population of parasites may undergo DV destabilization prior to mitochondrial depolarization.
evidence: This claim is inferred from LysoTracker experiments described in the text.

claim: LysoTracker Red accumulation in the DV was observed in parasites recovering from heat shock in the absence of LY294002.
source: We observed LysoTracker Red accumulation in the DV of parasites recovering from heat shock in the absence of LY294002, but not those maintained in the presence of LY294002 (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: 12 Plasmodium proteins co-precipitated with PI(3)P-conjugated beads.
source: We identified 12 Plasmodium proteins that co-precipitated with PI(3)P-conjugated beads (Table 1), among which three DV-associated proteins (PfRan, PfAlba1 and PfHsp70-1) (Lamarque et al., 2008) were selected for validation studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Table 1.

claim: PfRan, PfAlba1 and PfHsp70-1 are DV-associated proteins.
source: We identified 12 Plasmodium proteins that co-precipitated with PI(3)P-conjugated beads (Table 1), among which three DV-associated proteins (PfRan, PfAlba1 and PfHsp70-1) (Lamarque et al., 2008) were selected for validation studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lamarque et al., 2008.

claim: Direct interactions between PI(3)P and PfRan, PfAlba1 and PfHsp70-1 were confirmed.
source: Our experiments confirmed direct interactions between PI(3)P and PfRan, PfAlba1 and PfHsp70-1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein-lipid overlay assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PfRan, PfAlba1 and PfHsp70-1 did not bind to the control lipid phosphatidylinositol (PI) under the assay conditions.
source: Importantly, none of these proteins bound to the control lipid phosphatidylinositol (PI) under the assay conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by protein-lipid overlay assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: No PI(3)P binding was observed with PfHop.
source: Additionally, we tested another Plasmodium protein, PfHop, with no predicted PI(3)P binding as a negative control in the assay. No PI(3)P binding was observed with the same concentration of PfHop, suggesting the assay was detecting specific lipid–protein interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by protein-lipid overlay assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The three candidate proteins preferentially bound PI(3,5)P2 and phosphatidylinositol monophosphates including PI(3)P with different lipid-binding preferences.
source: Compared with 2xFyve, which binds to PI(3)P with a greater affinity than other lipids, the three candidate proteins preferentially bound PI(3,5)P2 and phosphatidylinositol monophosphates including PI(3)P with different lipid-binding preferences (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipid strip assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Mammalian Hsp70 homologs prevent photo-induced lysosomal membrane damage by associating with anionic membrane lipids.
source: Among the validated proteins, PfHsp70-1 was particularly interesting as its mammalian homologs prevent photo-induced lysosomal membrane damage by associating with anionic membrane lipids (Kirkegaard et al., 2010; Nylandsted et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on mammalian Hsp70.

claim: 15-DSG selectively binds to PfHsp70-1 over other Plasmodium Hsp70 homologs.
source: To test our hypothesis, we then probed the role of PfHsp70-1 with the small molecule inhibitor 15-deoxyspergualin (15-DSG) that selectively binds to PfHsp70-1 over other Plasmodium Hsp70 homologs (Ramya et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ramya et al., 2007.

claim: 15-DSG disrupts protein trafficking to the apicoplast.
source: 15-DSG is known to disrupt protein trafficking to another important PI(3)P-enriched organelle, the apicoplast, and to inhibit Plasmodium parasite loads, presumably via targeting PfHsp70-1 (Tawk et al., 2010; Ramya et al., 2007; Foth et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Parasites treated with 15-DSG exhibited destabilized DVs after 6 hr heat shock.
source: Here, we found that parasites treated with 15-DSG exhibited destabilized DVs after 6 hr heat shock, while the same treatment had no effect on the DV when cultured at 37°C, resembling the phenotype observed in PI(3)P-deficient parasites (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The LID domain of PfHsp70-1 has been previously shown to be the 15-DSG targeting site.
source: To investigate the correlation between reduced DV stability and the PI(3)P-binding capacity of PfHsp70-1, we generated a truncated PfHsp70-1 lacking the C-terminal LID domain. This domain has been previously shown to be the 15-DSG targeting site (Ramya et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ramya et al., 2007.

claim: Deletion of the LID domain disrupted the PI(3)P–PfHsp70-1 interaction.
source: Intriguingly, deletion of the LID domain disrupted the PI(3)P–PfHsp70-1 interaction (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), suggesting a mechanistic link between the PI(3)P-binding capacity of PfHsp70-1 and its ability to stabilize the DV under febrile condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: PfHsp70-1 is essential for intraerythrocytic P. falciparum replication.
source: In the presence of high aTc (50 nM), PfHsp70-1 expression is maintained and parasites replicate within erythrocytes (Figure 7—figure supplement 3). Upon aTc removal, PfHsp70-1 is depleted and parasite growth is substantially inhibited (Figure 7—figure supplement 3). These data indicate that PfHsp70-1 is essential for intraerythrocytic P. falciparum replication.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: PfHsp70-1-deficient parasites exhibited DV destabilization upon heat shock.
source: Upon heat shock, we observed that PfHsp70-1-deficient parasites (50 nM and 500 nM aTc) exhibited DV destabilization (Figure 7B), consistent with our 15-DSG data.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Heat shock did not cause mitochondrial membrane permeabilization in the PfHsp70-1 knockdown strain cultured in 500 nM aTc.
source: Importantly, the same heat treatment did not cause mitochondrial membrane permeabilization in the PfHsp70-1 knockdown strain cultured in 500 nM aTc, and only had a moderate effect when cultured in 50 nM aTc (Figure 7—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 7.

claim: Reduction of PfHsp70-1 levels in the conditional knockdown line (3 nM vs 50 nM aTc) induced hypersensitivity to both Wortmannin and LY294002 by 1.9–2.3 fold.
source: Additionally, reduction of PfHsp70-1 levels in the conditional knockdown line (3 nM vs 50 nM aTc) induced hypersensitivity to both Wortmannin and LY294002 by 1.9–2.3 fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: This change in drug sensitivity was not observed with Bafilomycin A.
source: This change in drug sensitivity was not observed with Bafilomycin A, a known anti-Plasmodium agent with a different mode of action (Figure 7C,D and Figure 7—figure supplement 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C, 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 8A.

claim: Bafilomycin A targets V-type H+-ATPase and inhibits Plasmodium DV acidification.
source: Bafilomycin A targets V-type H+-ATPase and inhibits Plasmodium DV acidification (Saliba et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Saliba et al., 2003.

claim: Hypersensitivity to Wortmannin and LY294002 was not observed in the control YFP line.
source: Furthermore, this hypersensitivity to Wortmannin and LY294002 was not observed in the control YFP line (Figure 7—figure supplement 8B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 8B and C.

claim: Suppressed PI(3)P synthesis causes the release of the protease cathepsin B from the lysosome in human vascular endothelial cells.
source: In human vascular endothelial cells, suppressed PI(3)P synthesis causes the release of the protease cathepsin B from the lysosome and in turn sensitizes cells to lysosomal-dependent cell death (Kirkegaard and Jäättelä, 2009; Madge et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on human cells.

claim: Inhibiting PI(3)P biogenesis impedes lysosomal function and leads to endolysosomal membrane damage in neurons.
source: Additionally, inhibiting PI(3)P biogenesis impedes lysosomal function and leads to endolysosomal membrane damage in neurons (Miranda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Miranda et al., 2018.

claim: Heat shock caused a 5.3-fold upregulation of pfhsp70-1 in P. falciparum.
source: A transcriptomic analysis revealed that heat shock caused a 5.3-fold upregulation of pfhsp70-1 and a 2.9-fold downregulation of a P. falciparum phosphoinositide phosphatase (PF13_0285) (Oakley et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Oakley et al., 2007.

claim: Heat shock caused a 2.9-fold downregulation of a P. falciparum phosphoinositide phosphatase (PF13_0285).
source: A transcriptomic analysis revealed that heat shock caused a 5.3-fold upregulation of pfhsp70-1 and a 2.9-fold downregulation of a P. falciparum phosphoinositide phosphatase (PF13_0285) (Oakley et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Oakley et al., 2007.

claim: pfpi3k and pfhsp70-1 seem to be co-upregulated in artemisinin-resistant strains.
source: Additionally, pfpi3k and pfhsp70-1 seem to be co-upregulated in artemisinin-resistant strains, collectively supporting a relationship between PI(3)P and PfHsp70-1 in response to cellular stresses (Tilley et al., 2016; Mbengue et al., 2015; Witkowski et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Artemisinin-resistant parasites usually have an enhanced ubiquitin–proteasome pathway concurrent with elevated PI(3)P levels.
source: In accordance with this hypothesis, artemisinin-resistant parasites usually have an enhanced ubiquitin–proteasome pathway concurrent with elevated PI(3)P levels (Paloque et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Paloque et al., 2016.

claim: Hsp70s can bind to exposed hydrophobic regions on unfolded/misfolded proteins to recruit E3 ubiquitin ligases for proteasomal degradation.
source: Moreover, Hsp70s can bind to exposed hydrophobic regions on unfolded/misfolded proteins to recruit E3 ubiquitin ligases for proteasomal degradation (McDonough and Patterson, 2003; Esser et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on Hsp70 function.

claim: Inhibiting PI(3)P production did not affect K48-ubiquitination levels in P. falciparum under heat shock.
source: However, our preliminary data showed that inhibiting PI(3)P production did not affect K48-ubiquitination levels in P. falciparum under heat shock (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bortezomib is a known antimalarial agent that strongly synergizes with artemisinin.
source: Bortezomib is a known antimalarial agent that strongly synergizes with artemisinin (Tilley et al., 2016; Aminake et al., 2012; Kreidenweiss et al., 2008; Reynolds et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inhibiting proteasomal activity caused a reduction in LysoTracker Red accumulation in the DV.
source: Interestingly, inhibiting proteasomal activity caused a reduction in LysoTracker Red accumulation in the DV (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), reminiscent of the increased membrane permeabilization observed in PI(3)P- and PfHsp70-1-depleted parasites under heat shock.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Plasmodium has conserved and functional ubiquitin–proteasome machinery with >50% of the proteome harboring at least one ubiquitination site.
source: Likewise, Plasmodium has conserved and functional ubiquitin–proteasome machinery with >50% of the proteome harboring at least one ubiquitination site (Aminake et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Aminake et al., 2012.

claim: PfHsp70-1 is crucial for nuclear-encoded protein trafficking into the apicoplast.
source: In P. falciparum, it has been proposed that PfHsp70-1 is crucial for nuclear-encoded protein trafficking into the apicoplast, another PI(3)P-enriched parasite organelle (Tawk et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tawk et al., 2010.

claim: Mutagenesis of putative Hsp70-binding sites within transit peptides reduced apicoplast protein translocation in P. falciparum.
source: Mutagenesis of putative Hsp70-binding sites within transit peptides, or PfHsp70-1 inhibition with 15-DSG, reduced apicoplast protein translocation in P. falciparum (Ramya et al., 2007; Foth et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PfHsp70-1 inhibition with 15-DSG reduced apicoplast protein translocation in P. falciparum.
source: Mutagenesis of putative Hsp70-binding sites within transit peptides, or PfHsp70-1 inhibition with 15-DSG, reduced apicoplast protein translocation in P. falciparum (Ramya et al., 2007; Foth et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A trial in Gabon showed that co-administrating naproxen and quinine did not interfere with parasite clearance by quinine.
source: A previous trial in Gabon showed that co-administrating naproxen (a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that relieves fever) and quinine did not interfere with parasite clearance by quinine (Lell et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lell et al., 2001.

claim: A study using a monoclonal antibody against tumor necrosis factor showed that fever reduction did not compromise parasite clearance by chloroquine in patients.
source: Another study using a monoclonal antibody against tumor necrosis factor (the primary mediator that induces fever) showed that fever reduction did not compromise parasite clearance by chloroquine in patients (Kwiatkowski, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kwiatkowski, 1993.

claim: Intravenous administration of ibuprofen in patients significantly delayed parasite clearance by artesunate-based combination therapy.
source: However, intravenous administration of the common nonsteroidal antipyretic ibuprofen in patients significantly delayed parasite clearance by artesunate-based combination therapy (Krudsood et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Krudsood et al., 2010.

claim: Artesunate may reduce heat tolerance in P. falciparum, perhaps through altered PI(3)P levels.
source: Our study may provide a plausible explanation for these seemingly contradictory results: artesunate may reduce heat tolerance in P. falciparum, perhaps through altered PI(3)P levels (Mbengue et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the study's findings and citation to Mbengue et al., 2015.

claim: Alleviating heat stress by co-administrating antipyretics may prolong parasite clearance by artesunate in malaria patients.
source: Therefore, alleviating heat stress by co-administrating antipyretics may prolong parasite clearance by artesunate in malaria patients.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the study's findings.

claim: P. falciparum 3D7 was cultured at 28–37 hr post-invasion (hpi) at 40°C for 3–12 hr, followed by recovery at 37°C for 45 hr.
source: Synchronized P. falciparum 3D7 was cultured at 28–37 hr post-invasion (hpi) at a physiologically relevant febrile temperature (40°C) for 3–12 hr, followed by recovery at 37°C for 45 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: >97% of the parasites were trophozoites even after a 12 hr heat shock.
source: We observed growth inhibition that generally correlated with the duration of the heat shock and no developmental arrest, as >97% of the parasites were trophozoites even after a 12 hr heat shock (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Trophozoite-stage parasites (32 hpi) were treated with Wortmannin (0.3–1.5-fold EC50 concentrations) and subjected to a 6 hr heat shock.
source: Trophozoite-stage parasites (32 hpi) were treated with the inhibitors (0.3–1.5-fold EC50 concentrations) and subjected to a 6 hr heat shock.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: No inhibition was detected in the negative control DMSO after heat shock.
source: No inhibition was detected in the negative control DMSO after heat shock, indicating an increased sensitivity to heat in PI(3)P-deficient parasites.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: LysoTracker Red normally accumulates in the Plasmodium DV.
source: Therefore, we used LysoTracker Red, which normally accumulates in the Plasmodium DV, to probe DV membrane integrity that is independent of protein synthesis and trafficking (Tomlins et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tomlins et al., 2013.

claim: Laser-induced DV photolysis can occur in Plasmodium parasites.
source: To complete this study, we first optimized our live cell confocal microscopy assay conditions to avoid laser-induced DV photolysis (Wissing et al., 2002; Rohrbach et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cell death in Plasmodium parasites is characterized by mitochondrial depolarization.
source: Cell death in Plasmodium parasites is characterized by mitochondrial depolarization, which can be detected as a decrease in the red-to-green fluorescence intensity ratio (Lee et al., 2014; Rathore et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The higher potency of Wortmannin relative to LY294002 in inhibiting PI3K activity may be a factor contributing to a more mixed phenotype.
source: The higher potency of Wortmannin relative to LY294002 in inhibiting PI3K activity may be a factor contributing to a more mixed phenotype (Vaid et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation based on known properties of the inhibitors and citation to Vaid et al., 2010.

claim: DV permeabilization is generally considered a lethal event.
source: DV permeabilization is generally considered a lethal event since it was assumed that the release of proteases and accompanying cytosolic acidification induces cell death (Porter et al., 2008; Ch'ng et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Saponin selectively permeabilizes the host erythrocyte membrane while maintaining the integrity of the parasite plasma membrane.
source: Fractionation of the intracellular P. falciparum erythrocytic parasites can be achieved with saponin, which selectively permeabilizes the host erythrocyte membrane while maintaining the integrity of the parasite plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about saponin fractionation.

claim: 2xFyve is a known PI(3)P-specific binding peptide.
source: The known PI(3)P-specific binding peptide, 2xFyve (Gillooly, 2000), was also purified in parallel for an assay control.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gillooly, 2000.

claim: The protein–lipid overlay assay is routinely used to qualitatively evaluate lipid–protein binding interactions.
source: This assay is routinely used to qualitatively evaluate lipid–protein binding interactions (Dowler et al., 2002; Pal et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 2xFyve binds to PI(3)P with a greater affinity than other lipids.
source: Compared with 2xFyve, which binds to PI(3)P with a greater affinity than other lipids, the three candidate proteins preferentially bound PI(3,5)P2 and phosphatidylinositol monophosphates including PI(3)P with different lipid-binding preferences (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PI(5)P and PI(3,5)P2 appear to be absent in Plasmodium parasites.
source: Notably, PI(5)P and PI(3,5)P2 (that were associated with PfHsp70-1 in vitro) appear to be absent in Plasmodium parasites (Tawk et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tawk et al., 2010.

claim: Both Plasmodium PI3K and PfHsp70-1 are predicted to be essential and multifunctional.
source: Unfortunately, studying this lipid–protein interaction in the cellular context is challenging given that both Plasmodium PI3K and PfHsp70-1 are predicted to be essential and multifunctional (Tawk et al., 2010; Vaid et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PfHsp70-1 is highly abundant and present in the parasite nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: Moreover, PfHsp70-1 is highly abundant and present in the parasite nucleus and cytoplasm (Cockburn et al., 2011; Pesce et al., 2008; Kumar et al., 1991), thus confounding a possible colocalization study.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Episomally expressed PfHsp70-1-mCherry was localized throughout the parasite cytoplasm.
source: Indeed, episomally expressed PfHsp70-1-mCherry was localized throughout the parasite cytoplasm, and we did not observe a detectable change in PfHsp70-1 surrounding the DV before or after heat shock (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The LID domain of PfHsp70-1 is the 15-DSG targeting site.
source: To investigate the correlation between reduced DV stability and the PI(3)P-binding capacity of PfHsp70-1, we generated a truncated PfHsp70-1 lacking the C-terminal LID domain. This domain has been previously shown to be the 15-DSG targeting site (Ramya et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ramya et al., 2007.

claim: A dose response analysis showed that 4.6 nM aTc resulted in 50% reduction of parasite growth in the PfHsp70-1 line.
source: A dose response analysis showed that 4.6 nM aTc resulted in 50% reduction of parasite growth, while no effect on parasite growth was observed above 12.5 nM (Figure 7—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4B.

claim: No effect on parasite growth was observed above 12.5 nM aTc in the PfHsp70-1 line.
source: A dose response analysis showed that 4.6 nM aTc resulted in 50% reduction of parasite growth, while no effect on parasite growth was observed above 12.5 nM (Figure 7—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Parasite viability in the PfHsp70-1 transgenic parasite was highly sensitive to heat shock even with up to 1 μM aTc.
source: However, parasite viability in this transgenic parasite (maintained in 500 nM aTc) was highly sensitive to heat shock even with up to 1 μM aTc (Figure 7—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Removal of aTc did not affect parasite loads at 37°C and 40°C in a control YFP parasite line.
source: In contrast, removal of aTc did not affect parasite loads at 37°C and 40°C in a control parasite line in which yellow fluorescent protein (YFP) expression is regulated by the same aptamer-based system (Figure 7—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The increased heat sensitivity in the PfHsp70-1 line compared to the wild-type and YFP strains was most likely due to a decrease in the basal expression level of PfHsp70-1.
source: Thus, the increased heat sensitivity compared to the wild-type and YFP strains was most likely due to a decrease in the basal expression level of PfHsp70-1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Treatment with PI3K inhibitors, but not control antimalarial compounds, sensitized the PfHsp70-1 line to heat shock.
source: Furthermore, treatment with PI3K inhibitors, but not control antimalarial compounds, sensitized the PfHsp70-1 line to heat shock, consistent with our findings in the wild-type 3D7 parasites (Figure 7—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 6.
